Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we all know AI can get expensive.
  • Also: Microsoft says its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
  • Sources indicate that earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

Industry observers note that if it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s major bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Sources indicate that software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Recent findings suggest that instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Sources indicate that then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new.

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically states, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving tech giant labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

I find it particularly telling that this is from the manufacturer that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

According to recent reports, microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the tech giant’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

This means the organization doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads.
  • According to recent reports, in a recent blog post, Signal president Meredith Whitaker outlined the potential threat AI assistants like Siri and Gemini pose to the platform's promise of privacy.
  • Sources indicate that signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads. Signal's end-to-end encryption keeps prying eyes out, but if you use agentic AI on your device, your chats may not be as locked down as you think.

According to recent reports, in a recent blog post, Signal president Meredith Whitaker outlined the potential threat AI assistants like Siri and Gemini pose to the platform's promise of privacy. Systems-level capabilities like Gemini Intelligence (on Android) and Siri AI's Onscreen Awareness (on iOS and macOS) scan your screen and may be able to capture data from Signal conversations in the process, which can then be used to perform tasks. Not only does this potentially expose your information, but that of other conversation participants as well. Whitaker notes that this leaves privacy protections outside of Signal's control because the platform cannot easily restrict AI access to the app.

Sources indicate that signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11. While Signal cannot guarantee that AI won't have access to your data, there are a few protections now available for those on iOS and Android as well.

The main workaround in Signal for now is to restrict screenshots and screen recordings inside the app, though this does not prevent AI agents from potentially grabbing content from other parts of your device. According to Signal's support documents, these protections will now be enabled by default on iOS 27 and Android with the latest versions of the Signal app.

In a recent development, consumers on iOS 27 can confirm or manually disable screenshot protection via Settings > Privacy > Block Siri AI. The compromise with this setting is that it also blocks you from taking screenshots of Signal conversations in the app and App Switcher, though you can disable it temporarily for 10 minutes if needed. On Android, Signal automatically engages the "Screen security" setting when it detects an AI agent attempting to access the screen. This, too, blocks screenshots inside the app and can be disabled via Settings > Privacy > App security > Screen security. Signal cannot block screenshots on macOS 27. However, users can add Signal to their Excluded Apps list via System Settings > Siri, which at least limits proactive access to conversations by Siri AI.

#188628. Two Budget Smartwatches That Make Perfect Gifts

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1467 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Two Budget Smartwatches That Make Perfect Gifts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you or someone on your shopping list wants a fresh smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from.
  • Recent findings suggest that luckily, you do have options.
  • Industry observers note that contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you or someone on your shopping list wants a fresh smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from. The problem is, a lot of them can be quite pricey. Apple's cheapest smartwatch, the SE 3, starts at $249, and its other selections only skyrocket from there. On the flip side, the risk in picking a smartwatch that's too inexpensive is that the manufacturer likely made a series of sacrifices to get the price that low. At a certain point, the tradeoff just isn't worth it.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, you do have options. There are two smartwatches on the market that aren't just cheaper than the competition, they're not even in the same ballpark. And while you shouldn't expect the same capabilities as you would on flagship wearables, these devices are perfectly usable, both as fitness trackers and smartwatches—all while spending well below $100 a pop. CNET put both smartwatches through their paces to make these determinations, so you know whichever model you get, you won't be picking up a wearable paperweight.

Industry observers note that contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter. Amazfit is its own company, and produces a wide selection of smartwatch options. The Bip 6 happens to be the company's latest budget smartwatch, with an MSRP of just $79.99. In most cases, a price that low would be a red flag for a smartwatch, but not in the Bip 6's case.

The Amazfit Bip 6 holds its own against other flagship smartwatches. That's true on a surface level: This watch looks your average smartwatch, rather than a cheap imitation. In fact, at first glance, I'd bet most people would assume the Bip 6 is actually an Apple Watch. It has a rounded square design with a large 1.97-inch display with a resolution of 390 by 450 pixels (though there's no Always-On display). This isn't a cheap display, either: Amazfit put an AMOLED screen on the watch, which looks great indoors—though CNET Labs struggled to see the screen in direct sunlight.

According to recent reports, where the Bip 6 really shines, however, is with fitness tracking. This watch supports GPS, which makes tracking outdoor runs possible without a smartphone. CNET Labs found that it takes about 10 seconds to find a GPS signal, but once it connects, you're set. While running, the Bip 6 reliably tracks your heart rate. CNET Labs compared its sensor to the Polar chest strap HR monitor and found it on par, though, like other smartwatches, the Bip 6 is slower at detecting heart rate spikes. You'll get data like cadence and stride while tracking runs, and strength training and muscle groups while working out indoors. For example, CNET Labs found that it correctly identified arm muscle exercises while testing the watch during a pilates session.

You also get some health and wellness features, too. The Bip 6 can measure heart rate variations, body temperature changes, sleep stages, and even your breathing quality. Its One Tap Measuring mode supports a single reading for heart rate, SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation), stress, and breathing rate, and it supports cycle tracking—though CNET specifies it can't track skin temperature like other smartwatches and health trackers. There's an optional subscription that provides AI coaching tools and looks out for health conditions like sleep apnea and insomnia. While health and wellness tracking is solid, note that CNET Labs found Amazfit's app, Zepp, to be confusing, since it simply displays your data without much context or explanation.

For an $80 smartwatch, the Bip 6 has an excellent battery life. CNET Labs found that the watch could be pushed to its limits—multiple workouts using GPS, heart rate tracking, keeping the display on during workouts—and still run for eight days before needing a charge. In fact, reviewer Vanessa Hand Orellana speculates you could push the Bip 6 to Amazfit's two-week battery life claim by limiting some of the most intensive settings and features. The only downside here is that there is no fast charging, so it will take about two hours to get back to 100%. But if you're only charging the watch once every week or two, that isn't much of a burden. There's also no charger in the box, so you'll need to use a separate USB-C cable.

Recent findings suggest that as a smartwatch, the Bip 6 can be a mixed bag. CNET found that the UI was clunky and sluggish, and the OS requires some user intervention before it's as usable as a standard Apple Watch or Galaxy Watch. While the watch has a voice assistant, Flow, CNET found it to be borderline unusable. However, CNET states Android users can reply to texts with a keyboard or dictation without needing the assistant. iPhone users can't do the same by default, but by downloading a third-party app, they can jerry-rig the watch to send and receive texts.

It has been revealed that based on CNET Labs' testing, the Amazfit Bip 6 is one of the best budget smartwatches you can buy. For $80, you get a reliable workout tracker that looks like most standard watches on the market. And while you're making some sacrifices at this price point, they're largely worth it for $80.

While the Amazfit is a good choice for both iPhone and Android users, the Galaxy Fit 3 might be the best choice for Samsung users. This isn't an option for iPhone users, and while it works with all Android devices, you get some Samsung-specific perks if you have a Galaxy phone.

The Galaxy Fit 3 is even cheaper than the Amazfit Bip 6: This watch is only $60, which makes it among the cheapest smartwatches you can buy. Now, this doesn't look like your average smartwatch. Samsung opted for a fitness tracker-like design, with a long 1.6-inch (40mm) AMOLED display. But for a fitness tracker/smartwatch hybrid, it's a solid look.

Recent findings suggest that in CNET's testing, one of the Galaxy Fit 3's biggest strengths is its battery life—though it pales in comparison to the Bip 6. When pushed to its limits, the Fit 3 can run three days in between charges, though Samsung claims you can get it up to 13 days with the right settings. While the Amazfit has it beat, the Fit 3 might sound like a dream compared to other smartwatches, even from Samsung. Unlike the Bip 6, the Fit 3 supports fast charging. You can fill the watch up completely in just over an hour.

CNET did find that the "smart" elements of this wearable were a bit lacking, however. The Fit 3 doesn't support voice dictation or mobile payments like other watches do, and unless you have a Galaxy phone, you won't be able to access the camera remote or sync your alarms. And while the Amazfit Bip 6's "Flow" is hardly reliable, the Fit 3 doesn't have an assistant at all. You can see incoming calls and decline (but not answer) them, and you can send prewritten responses to text messages, but not initiate them. Still, CNET found that Samsung added the essentials: You have an alarm, calculator, weather app, camera remote, and, of course, the Samsung Health app. (What kind of health tracker would this be without it?).

Sources indicate that CNET found that the Fit 3 is a reliable fitness tracker, particularly for $60. You can track over 100 different workouts, and the watch automatically logs exercises like runs, walks, rowing, and elliptical sessions—if you enable auto-tracking, that is. It also supports swimming with its IP68 water resistance rating. CNET Labs found that the heart rate tracking was "generally accurate" when compared to the Polar chest strap, though its slower with registering heart rate spikes. Interestingly, the heart rate tracker was a bit delayed in testing, but once CNET reviewed the data in the health app, the data had corrected to be largely accurate. You also get high and low heart rate alerts, though no ECG app. (The $249 Apple Watch SE 3 also omits this feature.).

Industry observers note that in CNET's testing, the sleep tracker on the Fit 3 was useful, if not entirely accurate. The watch can detect your sleep stages and look out for snoring using your Galaxy phone's mic. Like other health trackers, you get a sleep score, but CNET found it a bit inaccurate, since it rated a six and a half hour sleep session "Excellent" (91/100).

Still, the Fit 3 is really the only other smartwatch option at this price point that people should seriously consider. Until another tech giant drops a product around this MSRP, you have two solid choices in the Amazfit Bip 6 and Galaxy Fit 3.

Crypto trading still forces users to choose between convenience and control

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A candlestick chart on a dark screen highlights prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.
  • As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a new generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.
  • For years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A candlestick chart on a dark screen highlights prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.

As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a new generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.

For years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off. Centralized exchanges offer relatively straightforward interfaces, but users must generally trust those platforms to hold their assets. Decentralized alternatives allow traders to retain control of their funds, although navigating wallets, blockchain networks, gas fees and bridges can make the experience considerably more complicated.

That divide has become increasingly relevant as security breaches and operational failures continue to expose the risks of centralized custody.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge for developers is no longer simply to build decentralized trading infrastructure. It is to make that infrastructure accessible enough for users who have become accustomed to the convenience of traditional exchanges.

Sources indicate that london-based cryptocurrency trading platform Byrrgis is among the companies attempting to address that problem. Its public launch on November 24 introduces expanded cross-chain trading functionality, token analysis tools and a simplified wallet experience built around a non-custodial architecture.

It has been revealed that on centralized cryptocurrency exchanges, owners typically transfer assets into wallets controlled by the platform. While this arrangement simplifies trading, it also means customers depend on the exchange’s security practices, financial stability and withdrawal policies.

Non-custodial trading changes that relationship by allowing users to retain control of their private keys and authorize transactions directly from their wallets.

However, self-custody introduces its own challenges. Customers become responsible for protecting their wallets, understanding transaction approvals and navigating potential vulnerabilities in smart contracts.

It also does not automatically eliminate exposure to third-party infrastructure, particularly when trading involves cross-chain protocols or external liquidity providers.

The question is whether developers can reduce those operational barriers without introducing latest forms of dependency.

“Security and control over funds should not come at the expense of a simple trading experience,” noted Siraaj Ahmed, CEO of Byrrgis. “With our full public launch, we’re bringing together cross-chain trading, token analysis and portfolio management in one place, while allowing consumers to maintain control of their assets instead of handing them over to a centralized exchange.”.

One of the persistent usability problems in decentralized finance is fragmentation.

Industry observers note that trading assets across different networks can require separate wallets, native gas tokens and bridging transactions. Users may also need to understand which blockchain holds a particular asset before executing a trade.

Byrrgis is attempting to abstract some of that complexity through a trading interface supporting Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain and, according to the organization, Robinhood Chain.

Its cross-chain routing system is designed to let people initiate supported swaps with a single transaction signature rather than manually moving assets between networks.

A feature called Universal Gas is intended to remove the need to maintain separate native gas-token balances for supported transactions.

These approaches reflect a broader direction in blockchain development known as chain abstraction, where the underlying network infrastructure becomes less visible to the end user.

According to recent reports, yet simplifying the interface does not remove the technical risks of cross-chain execution. Routing systems, liquidity providers and smart contracts can still introduce points of failure, even when people retain custody of their wallets.

Another challenge facing cryptocurrency traders is the amount of information required to evaluate unfamiliar assets.

Market liquidity, trading momentum and on-chain risk indicators are often distributed across multiple analytics platforms, making comparisons difficult for less experienced users.

Byrrgis has incorporated a feature called Scout Score, which assigns supported tokens a rating between 0 and 100 based on a combination of on-chain risk, market momentum and tradability indicators.

The scores revision as market conditions change, offering a consolidated assessment alongside the platform’s token discovery tools.

Such systems may make complex information easier to interpret, but they also raise questions about transparency and reliability.

A numerical score can simplify research, yet its usefulness depends on how indicators are weighted, how frequently data is updated and whether the methodology can identify emerging risks.

A high rating should not be interpreted as a guarantee of safety or future performance.

Beyond cross-chain trading and token analysis, Byrrgis has introduced card-based cryptocurrency purchases, a redesigned wallet onboarding process and changes intended to improve swap execution.

The platform also includes tools for tracking holdings across networks and managing multiple positions from a single interface.

These additions illustrate a wider challenge for decentralized trading applications: competing with the user experience of centralized platforms while preserving the characteristics that distinguish self-custody.

#188625. Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales.
  • Industry observers note that while BNPL intends can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any substantial discounts.
  • Industry observers note that to be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the company is not uniquely misleading on this front.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales. As you're adding item after item to your cart during the sale, you might be tempted by offers for an "affordable monthly payment system." Also known as "buy now, pay later" (BNPL), the pitch is a tempting one: Buy what you need now, and pay later, "on your own timeline." But as convenient as it sounds, you should think twice before using buy now, pay later options, whether during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or at any other time.

Industry observers note that while BNPL intends can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any substantial discounts. Let's take a look at the hidden costs of BNPL, and why you're better off paying upfront for all your Black Friday purchases.

Industry observers note that to be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the company is not uniquely misleading on this front. The process is straightforward: you choose your items, select Affirm (a third-party lender) at checkout, complete a quick application, and receive an instant decision on your loan terms. Individual transactions initiated through Affirm are limited to $25,000, with a daily maximum of $100,000 across multiple purchases—but of course, your Black Friday splurge will be nowhere near that significant, right? (Right?!).

The main draw of these programs is the ability to "pay at your own pace." If you are required to pay a down payment, that is due at the time of the transaction. From there, your first monthly payment is usually due one month after your purchase is processed. Each following payment will be due one month later, on the same day of the month.

You can choose your own timeline, usually spanning 3, 6, 12, or 24 months, depending on the purchase amount and your creditworthiness. Unlike traditional credit cards, Affirm highlights you the exact payment amount and total cost upfront, and claims no hidden fees or compound interest.

You need a separate Affirm account in addition to your Amazon Prime membership. The application process requires basic information, including your name, mobile phone number, date of birth, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Affirm performs a soft credit check initially, which doesn't impact your credit score, though they may conduct a hard inquiry for some loans.

BNPL prepares are helpful if you really need to finance something significant, but whenever possible, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses.

It has been revealed that the ease of this sort of financing can make expensive purchases feel more affordable than they actually are. When you can buy a $1,000 tablet for "just $67 per month," it's easy to lose sight of the total cost, as well as your overall financial picture. In turn, this makes it all too easy to overspend on items you might not have purchased otherwise. You're better off taking a breath, stepping away from your shopping cart, and setting alerts to be notified when a product hits a price you can stomach, at a time you can afford it.

Despite what you may have heard in the past, BNPL providers may report to credit bureaus, meaning your BNPL purchases can in fact affect your credit score. For instance, all Affirm payments (including on-time, late, and missed payments) are now reported to the credit bureau Experian. So if you miss payments or default on the installment proposal, it will cause damage to your credit score—making it even harder to get approved for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and other financing down the road.

Still, not all BNPL providers report to credit bureaus or use the same type of credit check, so it’s important to understand the specific terms and practices of any service you’re considering.

According to recent reports, when you use a credit card, you get valuable purchase protections like extended warranty coverage, price protection, and the ability to dispute fraudulent charges. BNPL prepares generally don't come with these safeguards. This means you're on the hook if something goes wrong with your BNPL purchase and the retailer doesn't make things right. The smarter move is to only buy what you can afford during a sale, no matter how tempting those deals may seem.

Industry observers note that although installment intends are helpful if you really need to finance something major, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses. Better to wait for a good price for something you truly need and can afford to pay for right now.

If there's a significant-ticket item on sale for Black Friday but it's still out of your budget, consider these two questions before you turn to BNPL through Affirm:.

Is this really an essential purchase? BNPL should really only be used on completely necessary purchases that you can’t afford right now, but can afford in six weeks. On that note...

It has been revealed that will I be able to pay this off within six weeks? When a bigger payment gets broken down into smaller installments, you might find yourself overspending in the long run, because it "feels" like you can afford it. Stay on top of how much you’re actually spending—especially if you're considering multiple BNPL purchases—and how it will impact your overall budget going forward.

For more information about deals and discounts, keep an eye on all of Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage.

It has been revealed that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Recent findings suggest that follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Industry observers note that the best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sam Altman speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley conference, November 2026.
  • OpenAI has hired from the CIA and walls off parts of its offices with “tented spaces” and turnstiles, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
  • In a Massive Read for the Financial Times, Patrick McGee and Rafe Rosner-Uddin describe how Big Tech is catching up with spying by hostile governments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sam Altman speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley conference, November 2026.

OpenAI has hired from the CIA and walls off parts of its offices with “tented spaces” and turnstiles, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. Anthropic has recruited from the US intelligence community for “internal risk” roles that watch its own staff. Both are defences against state espionage, which the FT says now targets the biggest tech companies.

In a Massive Read for the Financial Times, Patrick McGee and Rafe Rosner-Uddin describe how Big Tech is catching up with spying by hostile governments. The paper cites a person familiar with each firm’s looks. At Meta, the Superintelligence Lab sits in a Menlo Park building that other staff cannot enter. Even senior vice-presidents need prior approval to visit, the FT reported.

According to recent reports, openAI hired Aristedes Mahairas, an FBI veteran of nearly 24 years, as its global head of corporate security in August 2025. Its board includes Paul Nakasone, a retired general who once ran the National Security Agency. At OpenAI’s offices, private and public meeting rooms sit in separate areas with different access rules, according to the FT.

“We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI noted in a statement to the FT.

Industry observers note that last year, Anthropic set up a national security advisory council that includes former senator Roy Blunt and David Cohen, twice a CIA deputy director. The firm told the FT it runs strict personnel vetting, access controls, and insider-risk monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that its filing with the SEC before last week’s listing names the threat directly. It also warns that state-backed actors and competitors could pressure staff after they join.

“We have been and expect that we will continue to be targeted by individuals seeking employment under false identities,” Anthropic wrote in the filing.

According to recent reports, in October, OpenAI’s security team found a recording device behind a television in a meeting room used by executives. It came wrapped in toilet paper, according to the FT, and the manufacturer called the FBI. Federal agents arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer and Saudi national, on wiretapping charges. He has pleaded not guilty, and his trial starts in January. His lawyers call him an “overly curious tinkerer” with no harmful intent. Sam Altman also spoke about the bug when he told a Semafor audience that OpenAI’s security had not been perfect.

Sources indicate that last week, the US Justice Department indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on four counts. Prosecutors say Russian handlers sent him to watch staff at a Silicon Valley technology and defence company because it supplied weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The department did not name the company. The FT identifies it as Palantir.

According to the Justice Department, D’iu photographed employees’ laptop screens in a coffee shop near the manufacturer’s Palo Alto office. He also followed one employee for nearly 30 miles. FBI agents later found a notebook with profiles of at least three staff, including their family members’ names and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses.

Nvidia is the third case. On Monday, its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, 11 days after he resigned. He had stepped down after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities consider a Chinese intelligence asset. China’s foreign ministry calls the allegations a smear. Nvidia’s board indicates it has no reason to believe anyone compromised national security or Nvidia’s secrets.

Greg Levesque runs Strider Technologies, a firm that tracks state-backed threats to companies. He told the FT that the Huang affair should wake up Silicon Valley.

“The biggest tech firms now operate on the scale of countries, and foreign intelligence services target them in the same way,” Levesque told the FT.

Sources indicate that D’iu remains in federal custody. The Justice Department listed his next court appearance for 24 November.

How Often You Need to Order From Amazon to Make Prime Worth It

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that black Friday isn't until Nov.
  • In a recent development, millions of Amazon Prime consumers right now pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other intends cost less if you qualify.
  • If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sales have been ramping up for several days. For frequent Amazon shoppers, Prime can rapidly pay for itself—mostly thanks to the free shipping perk. But how does the math shake out if you aren't regularly ordering from Amazon? Is it worth signing up if you only shop during major sales?

In a recent development, millions of Amazon Prime consumers right now pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other intends cost less if you qualify. For example, the Amazon Prime Student program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.

Here are the main perks of Amazon Prime that make it worth the cost for so many users.

Free two-day shipping on millions of items: This is the main draw of Prime. If you shop frequently on Amazon and want quick free delivery, the shipping perks alone may make Prime worthwhile. Prime members also get free same-day delivery on over 3 million items in eligible areas. The ultra-fast (and morally suspect) shipping usually costs $9.99 per order for non-members, though you can choose lower-cost or free shipping options if you're willing to place larger orders and wait longer to receive them.

It has been revealed that access to Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals. If you ask me, the content library isn’t as robust as Netflix or Hulu, but this is still an added value.

Other Prime benefits: You also get Amazon Music for streaming songs, Prime Reading for ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks; Prime gaming, free photo storage, and occasional exclusive discounts/deals.

Amazon Prime Rewards Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon/Whole Foods purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the annual fee.

Industry observers note that number of users: Prime benefits can be shared with other members of your household. The more users, the more value per person.

Let's say you don't care about Prime Video, Amazon Music, or free e-books, and just want to know if you'll save money you would otherwise be spending on shipping.

According to recent reports, for non-Prime members, Amazon requires a minimum order of $35 to qualify for free shipping on eligible items. The average shipping costs for non-members aren't publicly listed, and can vary by item and shipping speed, typically ranging from $5 to $10.

For our purposes, I messed around on my non-shared, non-Prime Amazon account to find an average shipping cost of around $6 per order (assuming the order total fell below the $35 threshold, of course). Of course, shipping costs will vary depending on the item and how swiftly you want it, but let’s compare the cost to the appeal of Prime’s two-day shipping option. So, we have the cost of individual online orders (around six bucks) compared to the free delivery that comes with an $139 annual fee. This means the costs you’d save on shipping alone make Prime worth the cost as long as you place more than two dozen orders in a year.

In other words: The $139 annual fee pays for itself as long as you order from Amazon Prime at least twice a month.

Sources indicate that of course, this conclusion is strictly in terms of shipping costs. How it stacks up ethically is between you and the person in the mirror.

And then there's this important caveat: You can still get free shipping from Amazon without a Prime membership, provided your order has $35 or more of eligible items. However, this won't grant you Prime shipping speed—your order will typically take five to eight days to be delivered. But you can place fewer, larger orders and wait a little longer, and still never pay for shipping.

It has been revealed that also worth considering is how much of that membership cost you'll be able to recoup via exclusive Prime Day offers. During the sale, some items will be heavily discounted only for Prime members—but whether the Prime Day price is really a "deal" will vary greatly based on the item you're buying. Some of those "big discounts" aren't any greater than what the item typically sells for. The Prime Day price can even be higher than other sale prices throughout the year. That's why it's key to make sure what you're ordering is something you planned to buy anyway—and that the sale price is actually a true bargain—before you order.

The cost of a Prime membership is a solid value for anyone using Amazon 23 times per year or more—especially if you're also watching demonstrates on Prime Video or purchasing something that is deeply discounted for Prime Day. But if you only shop on Amazon a few times a year and don't take advantage of Prime Day offers or the other benefits, then that $139 annual fee isn't necessarily paying for itself.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Sources indicate that nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026, plus more AI workplace updates

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella confirmed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft claims its newly introduced AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella confirmed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft claims its newly introduced AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several upcoming Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

“As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also announced Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft remarked, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s fresh Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft stated the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

Recent findings suggest that “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft remarked.

The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft stated of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

Microsoft also declared that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can promptly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft revealed a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Industry observers note that agent 365, which Microsoft declared last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft highlighted how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

In a recent development, “It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft mentioned. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft noted. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

#188616. Latest Update: I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (984 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts.
  • These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being.
  • Sources indicate that it's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra plans ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

Sources indicate that it's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Industry observers note that some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

In a recent development, there's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Industry observers note that someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Recent findings suggest that having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees.".

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

Unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

In a recent development, the best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

In a recent development, that said, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also shows just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (431 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service.
  • On Tuesday, Tidal declared looks to ban AI music from its platform entirely.
  • This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a upcoming uncontested winner: Tidal.

On Tuesday, Tidal declared looks to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal says it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”.

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the organization confirmed that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Recent findings suggest that robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the manufacturer's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

In a recent development, I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the tech giant could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies initiative to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your fresh pick.

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Recent findings suggest that situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It promptly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the latest social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the shows share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

The 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the massive city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their newly introduced home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated shows in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

It has been revealed that kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense upcoming forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

Former Vice President Al Gore has purchased the Carthage Courier, a 110-year-old weekly newspaper that covers his Tennessee hometown and surrounding area.

The current owners, the family of Hershel and Geraldine Lake, noted that the sale will be finalized in the coming weeks.

It has been revealed that gore said in a statement, “I’m so grateful to the Lake family for their decades of leadership in supporting independent news here in Smith County. Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community.” Related Stories News MS NOW Hosts Sign On To Letter Urging Adoption Of "Fair" WGAE Contract; Network Says Talks Are Ongoing And "Constructive" News Joe Rogan's The Most Trusted Name In Media For Dudes - Especially Dudes With Daddy Problems.

According to recent reports, gore stated that when the paper came up for sale, “I saw an opportunity to help preserve the Courier as an independent voice for Carthage and Smith County. I look forward to supporting the Carthage Courier team, many of whom have served this community for decades, as they continue to provide vital information and serve this community for generations to come.” Watch on Deadline.

Carthage is about one hour east of Nashville.

The publication also declared that Roger Wells would become publisher, succeeding Scott Winfree, who will serve in a part-time role as adviser due to health challenges. The Courier also remarked that the current staff would be retained.

Gore previously was co-owner of Current TV, the cable channel that initially specialized in user-generated content and later switched to news programming and a lineup of progressive hosts. The channel was sold to Al Jazeera Media in 2013.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.
  • Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos.
  • In a recent development, jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos. The Microsoft Code Red follows the global outage of 12 to 13 November. It knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about 24 hours.

In a recent development, jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, called it the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history. Never before had so many customers gone without email for so long, he told staff in a memo on Friday. The outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms, and disrupted airline communications.

“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.

Amanda Silver oversees M365 Core and Work IQ as a corporate vice-president. She described the response in a separate memo on Monday. Engineers worked through a “fog of war”, she wrote. Responders sent more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats.

Diagnostic data sat in separate internal tracking systems. As a result, the team struggled to keep one shared picture of its theories and decisions, Silver wrote.

Industry observers note that charles Lamanna is Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform. He told a Code Red review that the failed part had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures”, according to Silver’s memo.

Industry observers note that microsoft has blamed a dormant July defect in Windows for the outage, a scalability bug that went undetected for months. Chief executive Satya Nadella apologised publicly. Microsoft says cyber activity and AI agents played no part.

According to recent reports, silver set out five workstreams under the Code Red, covering load shedding, splitting traffic by region, and faster recovery. Microsoft wants to resolve future incidents worldwide within an hour. It also prepares to use AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster.

It has been revealed that henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, plus weekly reviews. Substrate runs the engineering behind Microsoft 365’s core services. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that its teams keep working around the clock to apply the lessons learned.

Earlier this month, Henderson wrote that urgent patches to M365 Core services took too long to reach owners worldwide. In one recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days. For the most urgent security challenges, he wants an hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. Microsoft is not there yet, he wrote.

Last week, Nadella said that AI-found bugs will make outages more likely. Henderson also wrote that he had reviewed the organisational and structural problems behind the failure.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson wrote.

Industry News: If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it.
  • Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not.
  • At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

Industry observers note that the film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a significant-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

In a recent development, if you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, the true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that if your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the organization lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.
