#188571. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3549 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • In a recent development, I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

In a recent development, I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

Recent findings suggest that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen reveals my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

In a recent development, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Sources indicate that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

According to recent reports, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

In a recent development, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

Industry observers note that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga states, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga states. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

According to recent reports, remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

According to recent reports, in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

Industry observers note that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Sources indicate that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Sources indicate that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

In a recent development, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

It has been revealed that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga claims.

Industry observers note that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell notes. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

It has been revealed that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Recent findings suggest that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

It has been revealed that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, states experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Industry observers note that medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra notes, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

According to recent reports, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

According to recent reports, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as swiftly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell notes. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy confirmed US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he states. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

In a recent development, the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga indicates they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How swiftly are doctors picking up on this upcoming technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print matter as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

Tech Report: Gemini's New AI Agent Is Surprisingly Useful (If You Use Google for Everything)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app.
  • To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat.
  • According to recent reports, of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all key emails, calendar appointments, and tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

According to recent reports, of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all key emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

While Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

Recent findings suggest that if you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free strategy only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini intends have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro users. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is right now live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

It has been revealed that some features, though, are only for U.S. owners. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Sources indicate that gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any notable steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free plan, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting owners to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip.
  • Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts people have saved into plans.
  • Muse launched in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for consumers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting owners to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip. Muse already worked in its own app, in WhatsApp and on Instagram profiles, and Meta states it does not read private messages unless users allow it, though Reuters reported staff found it reading encrypted chats.

Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts people have saved into plans. Meta revealed the change through Muse’s own Instagram account on Tuesday, using a long-planned trip as the example.

Muse launched in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for consumers. It works in its own app and in WhatsApp, and later that month users could add it to their Instagram profiles.

Sources indicate that the DM option puts Muse where the saved posts already sit. Meta has not said which countries get it. Beyond the US, Muse is live in Canada and has launched in Australia, and it reached the UK this week.

Messaging Muse does not give it access to private chats. Meta’s privacy page says Muse does not read private messages unless owners allow it through a connector.

It has been revealed that yet Reuters reported last week that Meta staff found Muse reading encrypted messages. Meta called those isolated incidents.

Customers can also make Muse ask before it sends messages or buys anything. In September, though, a YouTuber said Muse shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before asking him. Meta said it was looking into it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As summer draws to a close, the theatrical release of Children of Blood and Bone draws nearer.

The film adaptation of Tomi Adeyemi’s YA fantasy is directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood, and it stars quite a stacked cast of actors and characters.

For everything we know about the Children of Blood and Bone movie, read on.

When will Gina Prince-Bythewood’s Children of Blood and Bone come out?

The film will arrive in theaters January 15, 2027 as one of the first highly anticipated releases of the upcoming year.

It has been revealed that who is in the cast of the Children of Blood and Bone movie? Watch on Deadline.

According to recent reports, thuso Mbedu, who worked with both director Prince-Bythewood and costar Viola Davis on The Woman King (2022), will star as the main character Zelie. Amandla Stenberg (The Hate U Give, The Acolyte) will portray Amari. Damson Idris (F1, Snowfall) will play Inan. Tosin Cole (Supacell) will portray Tzain.

Sources indicate that davis will portray Mama Agba. Cynthia Erivo (Wicked) will portray Admiral Kaea. Idris Elba (Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw) will play Lekan. Lashana Lynch (Bob Marley: One Love) plays Jumoke, and Chiwetel Ejiofor (12 Years a Slave) plays King Saran. Regina King (Shirley) will appear as Queen Nehanda. Diaana Babnicova will portray Folake and Buuky Bakray will portray Binta.

According to recent reports, saniyya Sidney (Fences), Zackary Momoh (Harriet), Richard Mofe-Damijo (Namaste Wahala), Ayra Starr, Pamilerin Ayodeji (Mikolo), Shamz Garuba (Crime and Justice Lagos), Kola Bodunde (Shadow) and Temi Fagbenle rounded out the cast later on. Ayodeji and Garuba were cast through an open casting call in Nigeria.

Is there a trailer for the Children of Blood and Bone movie?

Yes, a trailer was released in late July, introducing the cast and their characters as Orïsha faces a battle for its magic. Another trailer was released in early November along with artists who have contributed songs to the film.

RELATED: Gina Prince-Bythewood’s ‘Children Of Blood And Bone’ Trailer Glimpses Thuso Mbedu’s Quest To Restore Magic To Orïsha.

What is Children of Blood and Bone about?

The first novel in the Legacy of Orïsha trilogy chronicles Zelie’s journey to restore the intrinsic magic to the land after King Saran made a move to purge it, seeing it as a threat and unnatural. Drawning on African mythology, the fantasy setting contains groups of humans that practice magic known as Maji. The Maji divine certain elements, and thus are known by the specific powers they wield, from water workers beckoning tides to those like Zelie’s mother Jumoke, who can summon souls.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Industry observers note that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic has opened Skills over MCP in public beta, letting apps that connect to Claude ship playbooks alongside their tools. Tasks, for long background jobs, and Elicitation, which pauses for user input, are now generally available, with File Uploads coming soon.

Industry observers note that apps that plug into Claude through MCP can now also tell it how to use them, Anthropic mentioned on Tuesday. The feature, Skills over MCP, is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code.

MCP is the open standard Anthropic launched two years ago to link AI agents to outside apps and data. Servers built on it already list the tools Claude can use. With skills, they can also ship step-by-step guides and best practices, which Claude loads only when needed.

It has been revealed that shopify uses skills to help Claude design and enhancement online stores, and HubSpot to onboard customers. Skills update with the server, so users have nothing extra to install. More apps are opening up, too: Canva opened its MCP server to all developers on Tuesday.

In a recent development, the beta is on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra looks. Team admins can switch it on, and Enterprise support is coming soon.

It has been revealed that two other features are now generally available. Tasks lets a server run long jobs in the background while Claude keeps working, which ZoomInfo uses for deeper research. Elicitation lets a server pause and ask the user for input.

In a recent development, gitHub, for example, makes users type a repository’s name before an agent deletes it. Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project. A fourth feature, File Uploads, will soon let Claude send PDFs, spreadsheets and images to servers.

The features are part of MCP, so servers that support them also work in other compatible apps. Anthropic says MCP now sees over 700M SDK downloads a month. In August, OpenAI and four rivals agreed on a standard for packaging skills and MCP servers.

Skills carry risks, too. That same month, researchers found malicious agent skills that stole passwords and keys after about 1.7 million installs.

In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.

1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

According to recent reports, the survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

It has been revealed that agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent users using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Sources indicate that retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Industry News: Andrew Garfield on Becoming Sam Altman in ‘Artificial’: ‘I’m Dying to Understand This Person’

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a tall order for an actor to embody any living person, but especially someone whom audiences may already have negative feelings about.
  • Rather than daunting, that challenge was “exciting” to actor Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI’s polarizing CEO Sam Altman in the film Artificial, slated for an initial Dec.
  • Garfield’s perspective on Altman morphed as he worked to better understand him, the actor told me ahead of an early screening hosted by SFFilm in the heart of the city where the story is set.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a tall order for an actor to embody any living person, but especially someone whom audiences may already have negative feelings about.

Rather than daunting, that challenge was “exciting” to actor Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI’s polarizing CEO Sam Altman in the film Artificial, slated for an initial Dec. 25 release. The biopic follows the rise of OpenAI, focusing on Altman’s relationships — particularly with his cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) — as he relentlessly pursues success amid Silicon Valley’s artificial intelligence power struggle.

Garfield’s perspective on Altman morphed as he worked to better understand him, the actor told me ahead of an early screening hosted by SFFilm in the heart of the city where the story is set. His mission as an actor is to get to the “central truths” of who a person is, he said, “and try to merge my soul with theirs. And like all of us, Sam has so many facets.”.

That includes physical traits. Garfield claims he had to lose weight and change his gait and voice to try to match Altman’s. The semblance is striking. From his bouncy stride to his clipped, gravelly speech, Garfield effortlessly emulates the Altman we’ve seen in interviews and Congressional testimonies. It’s a remarkable transformation — down to the sly, coaxing glint in his eyes — showcasing the breadth of Garfield’s acting talent.

Industry observers note that but it goes beyond physicality. Garfield had to dig deep internally to find elements “that felt like they were a match” with Altman, he said. The result is an astonishingly believable portrayal of a multidimensional figure, at once pensive and inscrutable.

Industry observers note that “There is a responsibility,” Garfield told me. “I take it very, very seriously to play any character, but particularly someone who’s alive, someone who’s pretty much my age. But also, maybe the greater responsibility is making sure that we interrogate these human beings that are leading our world into the next chapter, it seems.”.

“And it feels like our job as storytellers to reflect the times we’re in,” he added, “and no better way of doing that than by looking at the human beings — their personal relationships, their souls, all the diamond facets of their souls — and interrogate the people that have the power over our culture right now.”.

Industry observers note that artificial explores OpenAI’s rise through a rather bleak lens, with questions of moral responsibility and safety looming over the protagonists as they navigate the company’s success. The film is laced with dark satire, which offers moments of levity amid otherwise weighty meditations on the technology’s long-term impact.

In one scene, when Sutskever is asked about the difference between AI and artificial general intelligence, which can theoretically match or even surpass human ability, he plainly responds, “It’s like how rocket ships are different from scooters.” He goes on to tell his cohorts that this is achievable “in your lifetime — well, maybe not yours or yours or yours,” as he points to the less youthful figures in the room. Moments like these elicited generous laughter from the audience.

Director Luca Guadagnino, known for deeply character-driven stories, such as Challengers and Call Me by Your Name, mentioned he was following the news about Sam Altman’s temporary ousting from OpenAI in 2023 and was fascinated by the “Shakespearean feud” leading to that moment. Guadagnino applies his signature character-centric approach to OpenAI’s story, relying on slow, measured beats, piercing close-ups and suspenseful music to relay the stakes of each pivotal moment.

In a recent development, “It’s never about the object; it’s always about the people,” Guadagnino said during a panel discussion after the screening. “It’s not about AGI or AI. It’s about the conflict between worldview and way of being, embodied by people that clash or fight for the vision they have.”.

He also noted, “The point for me was more about trying to understand: How did the possibility of an incredible technology that can help all of us turn into the opportunity to get power in your hands and to become self-entitled?”.

Sources indicate that garfield is no stranger to portraying prominent figures in the tech world, having played Eduardo Saverin, Facebook’s co-founder and former chief financial officer, in 2010’s The Social Network. On the surface, Artificial seems like a spiritual successor, recounting another defining moment in the tech industry. But the films differ in both tone and approach, with Artificial trading rapid-fire drama for a darker, more existential theme that occasionally ventures into more technical territory. What the films do share is a focus on bold, forceful personalities.

Recent findings suggest that “From that experience, I suppose, I was very curious about what it takes to win in this particular late-stage capitalist world that we’re in with these emerging technologies,” Garfield said during the panel discussion. “What does it take to hold Sauron’s Ring of Power and not be completely burnt up by it? Is it possible to not completely lose yourself to that overwhelming, exponentially growing possibility and power?”.

It has been revealed that comic relief also arrives in the form of Ike Barinholtz playing OpenAI cofounder and tech mogul Elon Musk. By portraying him as a brutish, aloof figure who saunters in and out of rooms on a whim, he effectively underscores the absurdity of perceived importance and status. Almost every on-screen moment generated a murmur of laughter in the audience.

According to recent reports, “I think we’re all fascinated by these cultural, iconic figures who are leading us into this next stage of culture and society,” Garfield told the crowd. “They’re kind of kids. They’re kind of slightly stuck in an early developmental place, and that felt like a really notable part of Luca’s telling of this story.”.

In fact, he added, “[Guadagnino] would say to us, ‘This is a John Hughes movie. This is a high school, screwball comedy, just with slightly higher stakes — mixed in with a little bit of Invasion of the Body Snatchers.’ A very important part of this is that these are all kind of adolescent, high-school-minded people.”.

Even the way Garfield portrays Altman flippantly perching on couches and sitting cross-legged on tabletops while donning sunglasses — including during serious conversations about the future of OpenAI — was deeply researched.

“We had amazing consultants and researchers that work with us that gave us lots of information that’s not quite in the public arena about our characters,” Garfield remarked. “And Sam is someone who apparently would always sit like he was crisscross applesauce at play school, nursery school [or] kindergarten.”.

Ultimately, Artificial poses an open question about where society is headed and whether those at the helm are equipped to lead the charge. Amid weighty explorations of AI’s ramifications, the film paints a haunting, revelatory portrait of the cunning, mercurial figures making decisions that shape our world.

For Garfield, this presented an opportunity to dive deep into a figure like Altman, who, despite his prominence, remains largely elusive in the public eye.

According to recent reports, “I just wanted to tell this story and actually uncover for myself, excavate for myself, who is this person?” Garfield told me. “I’m dying to understand this person, and I get to try to understand this person, maybe more than anyone else has ever really tried to. And it feels like a gift to me.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that upcoming job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the firm has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced aims to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give owners more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

In a recent development, over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted newly introduced job listings that offer a closer look at its looks to develop autonomous AI agents:.

Industry observers note that in one, Apple remarked it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

According to recent reports, today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring owners to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the tech giant could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its intends for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how rapidly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally rolled out its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

Three of xAI’s co-founders have debuted Epochal, a startup that wants to teach AI to forecast events. Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss announced the company and its first product on Tuesday.

Industry observers note that its first product, Time Portal, lets AI agents browse the web as it looked at any moment over the past 30 years. Epochal says it covers more than 1 trillion pages, down to the minute on busy sites. A matching Linux sandbox sets its clock, software and downloads to the same date, so agents cannot spot the trick.

According to recent reports, to test it, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. Weeks later, it replayed the same questions through Time Portal. In its own test, the replayed forecasts closely matched the originals, with a correlation of 0.98.

Developers can try a limited version for free. Epochal has not said how it gathered the archive or whether the pages are licensed.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with upcoming privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several latest features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Apple is also introducing newly introduced tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful update, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and users on the public beta can now try out these newly introduced features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.
