💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts.
  • Industry observers note that airPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions.
  • Recent findings suggest that the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

Industry observers note that airPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

Recent findings suggest that the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

The key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

It has been revealed that if you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

Sources indicate that airPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

Industry observers note that if you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $149. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

According to recent reports, airPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

In a recent development, if you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

It has been revealed that are you planning to buy anyone AirPods this holiday season? Are they on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

#188499. Latest Update: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1413 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fzakaria ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fzakaria

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI.
  • I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables.
  • It has been revealed that turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

It has been revealed that turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲.

In a recent development, I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod!

Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

Recent findings suggest that the usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤.

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:.

The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

According to recent reports, the line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.

A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

In a recent development, on a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤.

Here is the whole output for libuv:.

Industry observers note that the second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief.

It has been revealed that in this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

In a recent development, the last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.

Recent findings suggest that for the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.

Sources indicate that --in looks inside one process,33It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line. so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep:.

According to recent reports, since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:.

🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds. It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case.

Sources indicate that as the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.

It has been revealed that the Rewind app’s Time tab highlights the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.

Industry observers note that clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and shows the stack where it slept:.

Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:.

If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope, or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev.

The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or open it on its own.

Recent findings suggest that every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer.55Bazel’s critical path analysis is a great example of this, and it has been around for years. I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in eBPF, back when flame graphs were latest. 🙇.

What Rewind adds is the data. Lots of it.

Sources indicate that rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch.

This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly.

It has just been a manic fever joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine.

Please accept rewind time as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg.

I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip revision, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

The latest Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the upcoming health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:.

The complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a latest Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

Most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

It has been revealed that more battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:.

In a recent development, I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off promptly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

I’m always on the lookout for something new to add to my Netflix watchlist, especially when there’s a good mix of psychological thrillers, gripping dramas and a little bit of horror.

Thankfully, the streamer’s latest top 10 list has a few titles that have caught my attention, including one particularly twisted psychological drama that feels like “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer's Body,” with a little bit of “Carrie” thrown in for good measure. If you’re anything like me and enjoy discovering your next binge-watch, these three demonstrates deserve a closer look.

Sources indicate that leading the way is a provocative teen drama about a group of Catholic schoolgirls whose spooky initiation takes a disturbing turn. There’s also a gripping limited series inspired by one of the biggest financial scandals in recent history, following two ambitious young entrepreneurs whose relationship and business empire spiral out of control.

Finally, a lavish historical drama returns for its third and final season, with complicated relationships and plenty of royal scheming.

Sources indicate that note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 indicates as of Tuesday, November 24, 2026.

Sources indicate that netflix’s current No. 1 show is “The Body,” a coming-of-age psychological drama that’s perfect if you enjoy your teen stories with a much darker edge. It’s been compared to “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer’s Body,” with shades of “Carrie” and “Yellowjackets” thrown in.

Creator Quinn Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell have also drawn on their own high school experiences and religious upbringing to give the story a more personal feel. It basically thrives on early 2000s nostalgia, which leans into what Shephard calls “gritty camp.” It’s a raunchy, unsettling teen drama, and certainly a little different from your usual coming-of-age stories.

“The Body” follows a group of students at an elite Catholic school whose lives take a disturbing turn after a Halloween party goes wrong. When the school’s all-girls dance team welcomes a newly introduced recruit, the group marks the occasion with an outrageous initiation ritual.

However, their night takes an unexpected turn when fellow student Grace (Sofia Wylie) falls into a coma. Anxious to avoid getting into trouble, the girls agree to keep what happened a secret. But when students begin reporting strange visions of Grace, rumors spread throughout the wider community, leaving the girls struggling to explain what they witnessed.

“The Altruists” is currently competing for the No. 1 spot on Netflix, and it’s easy to see why this real-life financial scandal makes for such compelling viewing. The biographical drama follows the rise and spectacular collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX, focusing on co-founders Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison.

Their relationship takes centre stage as an $8 billion fraud scandal sends shockwaves through the financial world. The show actually draws on public reporting, court transcripts and financial journalism to piece together the events surrounding FTX’s downfall. Fans of “The Dropout” and “Inventing Anna” should definitely have this one on their watchlist.

Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner) are two ambitious young entrepreneurs who set out to transform the global financial industry. After meeting in Upcoming York, the pair develop a romantic relationship while building their respective cryptocurrency businesses, with Sam at the helm of exchange FTX and Caroline running trading firm Alameda Research.

According to recent reports, as their companies attract billions of dollars in investments, their growing empire brings them extraordinary wealth and influence. However, behind the scenes, questionable business decisions and mounting financial problems threaten everything they’ve built.

Stream "The Altruists" on Netflix.

Finally, “The Empress” is another great Netflix historical drama to add to your watchlist, particularly if you enjoy lavish period pieces like “The Crown” and “Bridgerton.” This International Emmy-winning German series follows the life of Empress Elisabeth of Austria, with plenty of romance and bold costumes along the way.

The good news for fans is that season 3 was always planned as the final chapter, rather than being cut short unexpectedly. Creator Katharina Eyssen wanted three seasons to tell a complete story with a proper beginning, middle and end, giving the series a chance to wrap up its characters’ journeys.

Following the devastating Sardinian War, Emperor Franz (Philip Froissant) returns to Vienna a changed man, struggling with the loss of thousands of soldiers. His wife, Empress Elisabeth (Devrim Lingnau), tries to support him while fighting to save their fragile marriage.

However, Franz’s infidelity and growing tensions at court eventually drive Elisabeth to leave Vienna. During her journey, she meets Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin), a Hungarian revolutionary who quickly captures her attention. Meanwhile, Franz’s brother Maximilian (Johannes Nussbaum) travels to Mexico to claim the imperial throne.

Stream "The Empress" 3 on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, 9to5Mac is brought to you by Tello Mobile. Switching to Tello Mobile can bring the cost of your proposal down to as little as $5 a month, or an unlimited plan for just $25 a month, all on America’s largest 5G network. See all of the available intends at tello.com.

Among iOS 27’s many newly introduced features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces significant AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting new features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the patch also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

After iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most customers will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.
